card werk-hmr-swap-serve-reexec  [open]
The serve verb runs itself again under hot reload, and the child stops when its parent dies
why: A person starts the server with the plain serve verb, and hot reload is a runtime flag, not a setting a running process can turn on. So the verb starts one child with hot reload on, and the child alone holds the lock and the port. A parent that dies leaves no server behind that no one can stop.

To avoid a server that runs without hot reload, the serve verb starts a child process with hot reload on and waits for it. The child carries a marker naming its parent, so it never starts a child of its own. The child holds the lock and the port. The parent passes the stop signals to the child and exits with the child's exit code. The child checks that its parent is alive twice a second and stops itself when the parent is gone, so a killed parent never leaves a server that holds the lock. A person who starts the verb under hot reload by hand gets the server directly, with no child.

card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Research, two rounds of real-app testing, and a direct repro of the one open correctness concern settle it. Two priorities settle the rest: productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.
subtree: 5 cards, 1 open, 4 decided

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees the global object survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal harness shaped like werk's agent, pinned on the global object, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (an EADDRINUSE retry loop, then exit code 1). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): one guard clause in the server's start-up (a check, kept on the global object, that the server is not already running in this process) fixed both candidates identically. Both survive a real in-flight task through a source edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. Side effect worth knowing: this guard also means a hot reload stops applying code changes inside the start-up code - the tradeoff is 'my live session survives an edit' over 'my latest route-handler edit is live', which is correct for the original problem.

Runtime research (#werk-hmr:src4, Sept 2026): general research flagged one concrete objection to Bun as werk's runtime - oven-sh/bun #7716/#13811, open issues about SSE 'close' not firing reliably on client disconnect, which sounded like it hit werk's server directly.

Direct repro (#werk-hmr:src5): tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the exact version used throughout, and the one the research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to werk's actual live-stream handler and disconnected SSE clients both cleanly and via kill -9. close fired correctly every time, the client left the server's client list, no leak. The bug is real and filed, but does not reproduce for werk's specific pattern.

Decided: move werk's runtime to Bun (bun --hot). The one concrete correctness objection did not reproduce on werk's own code on the exact version tested

card werk-hmr-swap-serve-reexec  [decided]
The serve verb runs itself again under hot reload, and the child stops when its parent dies
why: A person starts the server with the plain serve verb, and hot reload is a runtime flag, not a setting a running process can turn on. So the verb starts one child with hot reload on, and the child alone holds the lock and the port. A parent that dies leaves no server behind that no one can stop.

`#werk-hmr-swap-serve-reexec` is now decided, and the code matches it. The card said the plain `serve` verb re-runs itself under `bun --hot`, but the code had no such step.

**What the code does now.** A plain `serve` starts one child with `bun --hot`. The child carries `WERK_HOT_PARENT=<parent pid>`, so it never starts a child of its own.
- The parent passes SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP to the child, and exits with the child's exit code.
- The child checks the parent twice a second and exits when the parent is gone.
- A serve started by hand under `bun --hot`, as `npm run dev` does, serves directly with no child.

**What I checked.**
- 9 new unit tests pass. The typecheck and the linter report no problems. I did not run the full test suite or the coverage gate.
- I started `serve` on port 4377. The process list showed the parent and a child running `bun --hot`.
- `kill -9` on the parent left no process and no `serve.lock` behind. A plain `kill -TERM` on the parent stopped the child the same way.

**Recorded on the card.**
- A `depends_on` edge to `#werk-onelock-take`.
- A manual kill criterion that repeats the SIGKILL check.
- I could not add an edge to `#werk-hmr-swap`, because it is already the parent of this card.

**Not done.**
- `src/test/pure-files.txt` now lists `src/hot-reexec.ts`. I never ran it against the 90% gate.
- 12 or more old `bun --hot … serve --port 0` processes are still running from earlier e2e runs, started from `werk-serve-*` temp folders, with parent pid 1. I did not start them and did not kill them. They show the orphan case this card is meant to prevent. Whether the e2e harness should start servers this way is a separate question.
